segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those who are not, and not please ourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each of us should please our neighbor for their good, to build them up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ also did not please himself; rather, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another, in keeping with Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that together, with one voice, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, to the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I say that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised for the sake of God’s truthfulness, to confirm the promises made to the fathers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again it says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples praise him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again Isaiah says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I myself am convinced about you, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able also to admonish one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I have written to you rather boldly on some points, by way of reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving the good news of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, made holy by the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to boast about what relates to God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and around as far as Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the good news of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in this way I make it my ambition to proclaim the good news not where Christ has already been named, so that I do not build on someone else’s foundation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Those who were never told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is also why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, since I no longer have room in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whenever I travel to Spain—for I hope to see you as I pass through and to be sent on my way there by you, once I have first enjoyed your company for a while—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but now I am going to Jerusalem in service to the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to share something of their own with the poor among the holy ones in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were pleased to, and indeed they are in their debt; for if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to minister to them in material things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when I have completed this and have delivered this fruit to them under my seal, I will set out for Spain by way of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge you, brothers and sisters, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that I may be rescued from the disobedient in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the holy ones,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that by God’s will I may come to you in joy and find rest in your company.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

notes.note: The traditional rendering is ‘for the truth of God’. In the Greek Scriptures this word often describes God’s reliability in keeping his word, and the next clause, about confirming the promises, shows that this is the sense here. Several modern translations render it similarly.

notes.phrase: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy
notes.traditional: and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy
notes.note: The grammar linking this clause to verse 8 is disputed. It is taken here as a second purpose of Christ’s becoming a servant, alongside confirming the promises. It can also be read as a second thing Paul asserts: ‘I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcised... and that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy’.

The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. The same word stands behind every ‘Gentiles’ in this chapter. In the Scriptures Paul quotes in verses 9–12 it could equally be rendered ‘nations’, and Paul’s argument depends on hearing it as the same word throughout.

The quotation is Isaiah 11:10 in its Greek form. Jesse was the father of King David, so the phrase points to the expected king from David’s line. The verb translated ‘rises’ is also the ordinary word for rising from the dead, and Paul’s readers may have heard that overtone.

The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole assembly, which chapter 16 shows included many women. Many modern translations render it this way, while others keep ‘brothers’.

The traditional rendering is ‘gospel’. The Greek word was an ordinary one for an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler’s accession, and the Greek version of Isaiah uses the related verb for the announcement of God’s reign. ‘Gospel’ is an old English word with the same meaning, but it now sounds like a religious technical term.

Paul describes his mission in the language of temple worship: ‘minister’, ‘serving as a priest’, ‘offering’, ‘acceptable’ and ‘made holy’ are all terms used of sacrifice. Most interpreters take the phrase to mean that the Gentiles themselves are the offering Paul presents to God. It can also mean the offering the Gentiles bring, which is their worship and obedience.

The manuscripts differ here. Many, including some early ones, read ‘the Spirit of God’, and others read ‘the Holy Spirit’. The edition translated here prints the shortest reading, ‘the Spirit’, and the meaning is the same in each case.

notes.traditional: whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you
notes.note: Paul’s sentence, begun in verse 23, breaks off here and is never completed. He interrupts himself to explain his hope and then turns to the Jerusalem journey. Later manuscripts add ‘I will come to you’ to repair the grammar, and many translations smooth the sentence in other ways. The break is left visible here.

The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the language of the Greek Scriptures for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’, and others use ‘God’s people’.

notes.phrase: delivered this fruit to them under my seal
notes.note: Literally ‘having sealed this fruit to them’. The ‘fruit’ is the collection of money. The image is probably commercial: goods were sealed to guarantee that they arrived intact and to mark the transfer as complete, so the sense is that Paul will see the gift securely and formally handed over. The exact force of the idiom is uncertain.

notes.traditional: unbelievers / those who do not believe
notes.note: Many translations have ‘unbelievers’. The Greek verb means to refuse to comply or be persuaded, and Paul uses it elsewhere in Romans for refusal of the good news, in contrast to the ‘obedience’ of verse 18. He is referring to people in Judea who reject the message about Christ, so in practice the two renderings point to the same group.

candidates.reason: It occurs throughout the New Testament and the choice between ‘gospel’ and ‘good news’, together with the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι, must be uniform or readers will think two different things are meant.
The plural address to mixed assemblies recurs in every letter, and translators divide between ‘brothers’ and ‘brothers and sisters’.
It ranges over fellowship, partnership, sharing and contribution across Paul, Acts and 1 John, and the link with the verb κοινωνέω is easily lost without a policy.
Translators vary between comfort, encouragement, consolation and exhortation, and the related verb παρακαλέω (urge, encourage, comfort) needs coordinating with it.
It is rendered variously as patience, endurance, perseverance or steadfastness across the letters and Revelation, and one choice would keep a key virtue recognisable.

warnings: Verse 13: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
